Hi there, I'm Emma!

Whenever I'm not pretending to be an elite runner, I am a PhD student at the UCL Econ Department - which mostly means running regressions instead of marathons. I also spent summer 2026 with Amazon's Economist Team in London. Check out my [research](/research/) or my [CV](/cv.html), and feel free to get in touch via email.

## Selected research

### [Less to Lose: How shorter and more flexible degrees reshaped university choice and earnings](/research/01_pt_bologna/)

**2026 UniCredit Foundation Best Paper Award in Education Economics**

University is risky when students can invest several years and still leave without a qualification. Portugal's Bologna reform introduced a credible three-year credential within longer degree paths, giving students an earlier exit and less to lose from enrolling. Using a cohort-based regression discontinuity design, I find that university completion rose by 8-9%, especially among women. Students shifted toward reformed fields such as STEM and economics and away from healthcare, where degree length did not fall. About 30% of the wage gain comes from sorting into better firms. Cumulative earnings dip in the twenties, while students remain in education, but rise above the pre-reform path by the early thirties.

[Paper](/papers/BP_Portugal_Scandolo.pdf) · [Slides](/papers/BP_Portugal_Scandolo_Slides.pdf)

### [Unpacking Successful Literacy Interventions: Evidence from Liberia](/research/04_lib_mechanisms/)

*With Pedro Carneiro, Nathalie Lahire, and Federico Tagliati*

Why do some literacy programmes deliver large learning gains? EGRA Plus Liberia combined intensive teacher training, coaching, and instructional materials with parental and community engagement. In a cluster-randomized evaluation, the full programme raised reading skills by nearly one standard deviation. A latent-factor model shows that 43% of the impact operates through improved teaching practices and school inputs, with a further 13% working through parental investments. The lighter parent-and-community intervention produced no lasting improvements on its own. The gains were specific to literacy, with neither spillovers nor crowding out in numeracy. The results point to sustained pedagogical support, reinforced by a stronger home-learning environment, as the key to successful literacy policy.

[Paper](/papers/EGRA_Liberia_2026.pdf)
